slides.heading: Properties of the Noun
bullets: A noun has four Properties:  Gender, Person, Number, and Case.
Gender — whether it names a male, a female, both, or neither.
Person — whether it is the speaker, spoken to, or spoken of (usually third).
Number — one, or more than one.   ·   Case — its relation to the other words.

slides.heading: Gender
bullets: Gender is a distinction of nouns with regard to sex.
Masculine — males:  boy, king, actor.   ·   Feminine — females:  girl, queen, actress.
Common — either:  parent, child, cousin.   ·   Neuter — neither:  house, book, stone.
Tell male from female three ways: different words (father/mother), endings (actor/actress), or a joined word (he-goat/she-goat).

slides.heading: Practice — What Gender?
slides.instruction: Tell the gender of each noun: masculine, feminine, common, or neuter.

slides.heading: Number & Forming Plurals
bullets: Number tells one (singular) or more than one (plural).
Most add s or es:  book→books, box→boxes.   ·   y after a consonant → ies:  mercy→mercies.
f or fe → ves:  knife→knives.   ·   o after a consonant → oes:  hero→heroes.
Irregular:  man→men, ox→oxen, goose→geese, child→children.   ·   Same:  sheep, deer.
Compounds pluralize the main word:  brothers-in-law, courts-martial.

slides.heading: Practice — Write the Plural
slides.instruction: Write the plural of each noun.

slides.text: Case is the relation of a noun or pronoun to the other words in a sentence.
examples: four cases: nominative, possessive, objective, absolute

slides.heading: The Four Cases
bullets: Nominative — used as the subject or predicate:  “Boys skate.”  “Horses are animals.”
Possessive — shows ownership:  “John’s hat,” “the sun’s rays.”
Objective — object of a verb or preposition:  “Indians hunt buffaloes,” “over the bridge.”
Absolute — used independently:  “James, bring a book.”  “Oh, my son!”

slides.heading: Practice — Which Case?
slides.instruction: Tell the case of the noun in parentheses: nominative, possessive, objective, or absolute.

slides.heading: Declension
bullets: Declension is naming a noun’s forms for number and case.
Boy — Nom.: boy, boys   ·   Poss.: boy’s, boys’   ·   Obj.: boy, boys.
Only the possessive changes its spelling; the nominative and objective look alike.
The nominative absolute has the same form as the nominative.

slides.heading: Parsing a Noun
bullets: To parse a noun, tell everything about it: part of speech, class, gender, person, number, case, and the rule.
Order:  noun → common or proper → gender → person → number → case → rule.
Model — “Wheat is a vegetable.”  Wheat is a noun; common; neuter; third person; singular; nominative case (the subject).
Parsing simply puts together all the properties you have learned.

items: What are the four properties of a noun?
What case is a subject in?
What case is the object of a verb or preposition in?
answers: Naming a noun’s forms for number and case.
Telling a word’s part of speech, properties, and use.
